terms.def: A military alliance of 32 countries in North America and Europe. Members promise to defend each other if one is attacked (Article 5).
The European Union: 27 European countries that share a single market, many common laws and, for 20 of them, the euro.
The United Nations: 193 member countries that meet to discuss peace, development and human rights. Its General Assembly gives every country one vote.
The UN body for peace and security. Its 5 permanent members (China, France, Russia, UK, US) can each veto a decision.
A group of large emerging economies, first Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, now expanded. It meets yearly to coordinate on trade and finance.
Seven large advanced economies (Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, UK, US) whose leaders meet each year. The EU also attends.
19 major economies plus the EU and the African Union. Together they make up most of the world's economy and trade.
An informal partnership of Australia, India, Japan and the US focused on a free and open Indo-Pacific. It is not a military alliance.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations: 11 countries that cooperate on trade, security and diplomacy in Southeast Asia.
The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation: China, Russia, India, Pakistan, Iran, Central Asian states and others cooperating on security and trade.
A union of 55 African countries that works on peace, integration and development across the continent. It is a full member of the G20.
Oil-exporting countries, led by Saudi Arabia and Russia, that agree how much oil to produce to influence world prices.
The Collective Security Treaty Organization: a Russia-led military alliance with several former Soviet states. Armenia has frozen its participation.
The International Monetary Fund lends to countries in financial trouble and tracks the health of the world economy.
A global lender that funds long-term development projects such as roads, schools and power in poorer countries.
Being able to launch nuclear weapons from land (missiles), sea (submarines) and air (bombers), so no single attack can remove them all.
The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty: most countries promise not to build nuclear weapons; five recognised nuclear states promise to work towards disarmament.
Preventing an attack by making sure the attacker expects the cost to be greater than any gain.
An agreement to stop fighting, often temporary. It is not the same as a peace deal, which settles the dispute.
The military line dividing the parts of Kashmir held by India and Pakistan. It is not an agreed international border.
A war in which outside powers support opposite sides with money, weapons or advisers instead of fighting each other directly.
A ban on selling or sending weapons to a country or group, set by the UN, a bloc or a single government.
A formal agreement in which countries promise to help defend each other, such as NATO.
When a state declares another country's territory to be its own, usually by force. Most countries refuse to recognise annexations made by force.
Gross domestic product: the total value of goods and services a country produces in a year. The usual measure of an economy's size.
How much GDP rose or fell compared with the year before, after removing price changes. Negative growth means the economy shrank.
How fast prices rise. 5% inflation means something that cost 100 a year ago now costs about 105.
The share of people who want a job and are looking for one but cannot find work.
Exports minus imports. A surplus means a country sells more abroad than it buys; a deficit means the opposite.
A tax on goods coming in from another country. It makes imports dearer and is often used in trade disputes.
Government debt compared with one year of the country's output. 100% means the debt equals a whole year of GDP.
An emergency IMF loan to a country that cannot pay its bills, usually with conditions such as cutting spending or raising taxes.
A period when the economy shrinks, often defined as two quarters in a row of falling GDP. Jobs and incomes usually fall too.
Penalties such as trade bans or frozen assets that countries impose to pressure another government, company or person.
A narrow sea passage that much of the world's shipping must pass through, such as the Strait of Hormuz or the Suez Canal.
Liquefied natural gas: gas cooled into a liquid so it can be shipped by tanker instead of sent through a pipeline.
The share of a country's energy that it must buy from abroad. High dependence makes it sensitive to supply shocks and prices.
Minerals such as lithium, cobalt and nickel that batteries, electronics and clean energy need, and whose supply is concentrated in few countries.
17 metals used in magnets, phones and weapons. China mines and processes most of the world's supply.
The part of a country's energy or electricity that comes from sources such as solar, wind and hydropower.
